notes: None of the four sources puts the question whether the avarız fund was a legal person distinct from the residents. Kars 164 gives only the DİA definition of vakıf as property withdrawn 'Allah'ın mülkü olarak temlik ve temellükten ebediyen' - a statement about property, carried at LP2. The nearest datum runs against personhood without being a statement about it: when a borrower died, 'Mütevelli de diğer alacaklılar gibi bir alacaklıdır' (Kıvrım 38, after Akgündüz 228-229), which names the trustee, not the fund, as the creditor. Silence, not an observed absence; 0 not coded.

Half-present, on the waqf_khayri pattern. Property is attributed to the fund: a house 'Avarıza ait olduğu daha önce ispatlanan' (Kars 183), a plot 'avarız vakfına ait olan' (Kars 181-182), cash that is the 'hâne-i avârızı vakfı olan nukûd' of a named quarter (Kıvrım Ek, 43-47), purchases 'vakıf adına' (Kars 180). But every acquisition, sale-and-leaseback and lease is made by or to the mütevelli (Kars 176-184), and the doctrine Kars 164 relays treats endowed property as withdrawn from ownership altogether. Held in the fund's name and owned by no one. Alternative: 1, if holding in the fund's name is read as holding as the entity. SUB-POOL: in Ayntab the quarter's cash is held per bölük/hane under separate mütevellis (Kıvrım 39, 45-47); the value is read at the level of the mahalle arrangement, not of a bölük.

Standing is exercised by the trustee in right of his office. The İbn Şeker mütevelli pleads the debt 'tevliyetim hasebiyle' - by reason of my trusteeship (Kıvrım 38, quoting GŞS 33-328/2); the Tövbe and Tarlayıatik mütevellis prove unpaid loans against heirs and obtain orders (Kıvrım 38); a new mütevelli's statement of a debt is contested and corrected before the kadı (Kars 182); residents of one quarter litigate its avarız revenue against another (Kars 174). No record shows the fund suing as an entity distinct from its officer. P = standing present, running through the office. Alternative 1. Articulated on the trustee's own formula, 'tevliyetim hasebiyle'.

Not addressed: no source describes creditors of the fund or ranks them against residents' personal creditors in its assets; the fund appears only as a lender. The one priority statement concerns a different question - when a borrower died 'vakıf alacağının diğer alacaklardan da farklı bir imtiyaz hakkı yoktu' (Kıvrım 38; Kars 182, in Kıvrım's words; both after Akgündüz 228-229): the fund as creditor had no priority in the debtor's estate. Carrying that across would make AP1 answer the reverse question.

Members' limb partly evidenced, creditor limb silent. The principal was not to be spent ('ana kaynağa dokunulmamış olurdu', Kars 167; Kars 179; 'Ana paradan harcama yapılmaması esası benimsenmiştir', Küçük 151), and the kadı instructs the trustee to lend the remainder 'asl-ı mâl olmak üzere' (Kıvrım 48) - rules about spending principal rather than about a member forcing partition. Whether residents' creditors could reach or divide the fund is never asked. One limb answered and one unevidenced is .NR on the house rule.

CF1 is 0, so the locator reverts to members (the residents). Whether a creditor of the fund could reach a resident's estate is not addressed; the fund has no described creditors. Residents paid the unfunded remainder of the levy among themselves (Kars 167; Kıvrım 37), but that is their own tax liability, not liability for the fund's obligations. Silence, not 0.

Founder-endowed: the corpus is constituted by identifiable donors' endowments out of their own property - Mehmed Efendi b. Rüstem Ağa's 36,000 akçe nukud vakfı (Kars 175), Emine Hatun selling her house and endowing the price to the Atik Ali Paşa avarız (Kars 176, 181), Fatıma's 5,000 akçe (Kars 176), Ayntab donors of 10 to 200 kuruş and of houses (Kıvrım 37-38), a property whose muaccele passes to the mahalle avarız when the founder's line fails (Gürsoy 98 n.8), a founder named in the Kırkçeşme vakfiye (Küçük 163). Founders are plural and cumulative; the locator is met donor by donor. Within-deed variants recorded and not coded: life occupancy of the endowed house reserved to the founder (Aynî Hatun and Hatun, Kıvrım 37-38); two donors' condition that their own houses pay no avarız (Kıvrım 37); a testamentary endowment revocable while its founder lived (Gürsoy 113, a general EMM finding, not avarız-specific). Capital also came as residents' contributions and sadaka (Kıvrım 37; Küçük 152, 157), which is still donation. EXPOSURE: the bundle's AP4 definition implies that one form under re-coding carries AP4=1 in the live file (priors, exposure item 1); this value was reached from the deeds cited.

Survives the death and exit of trustees and residents: mütevellis replaced on death, hajj, old age and neglect (Kars 173-174); ten mütevellis serve the Kırkçeşme fund 1834-1851 and it continues to 1867 (Küçük 160-161); Ayntab funds endowed from 1605 are audited as going concerns in 1692 (Kıvrım 37, 39).

No term and no single venture: endowment 'ebediyen' (Kars 164, relaying the DİA definition), principal worked without end to meet recurring levies (Kars 179), one fund's accounts running 33 years (Küçük 155).

Whether an avarız fund could be dissolved or unwound at will is not addressed. Gürsoy 113 shows a testamentary waqf revocable (rücu) by its founder while alive; that is a rule about one endowment before it binds, drawn from the EMM sample generally, and concerns a single deed, not the mahalle arrangement. Kars 175 reports founders' conditions written so that later guardians could not interfere, which bears on TS4. Not 0.

Half-present: the application of income could be redirected by the quarter's own decision; the corpus and founders' conditions could not. 'zamanla vakıf gelirleri köy, mahalle heyet kararıyla uygun yerlere sarf edilmesi usulü getirilmiştir' (Kars 168 = Kıvrım 35, both relaying İpşirli, DİA IV, 109 - one witness, not two); funds shaped 'mahalle ve köy sakinlerinin istişaresi sonrası' to new needs (Küçük 152); after the levy lapsed income went to quarter needs (Kıvrım 37); in practice sums were redirected to religious needs and to the poor's 1866 avarız (Küçük 161, 179). Against: founders fixed conditions so that no later party could alter them (Kars 175), and lending ran under kadı supervision (Küçük 151). Low, because the general statement rests on one encyclopedia entry relayed twice. Alternative 1. EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not 1 (priors, exposure item 3).

One pooled fund per quarter: 'her mahalle paylarına düşen avarız vergisi borcu için ortak bir bütçeyle avarız vakfı kurmaktaydı' (Kars 174); several endowments for the same mahalle 'avarız sandıklarında toplanarak' formed a fund (Gürsoy 105); the sandık as a fund for collective expenditure (Küçük 153). SUB-POOL, carried here and not coded: in Ayntab the Ammu fund is split into nine bölük/hane funds and Alineccar into two, each with its own mütevelli, ledger and capital earmarked for that bölük's avarız (Kıvrım 39, 45-47). On the 2026-08-31 rule the arrangement is the quarter's fund and these are internal partitions: on its sources' own enumeration the form is a sub-pool form in Ayntab and an aggregating one in Istanbul. Kırkçeşme's several mütevellis each holding bonds for a lending group (Küçük 156, 181) divide the administration of one capital, not the capital.

Contributed capital stays in: spending is from profit only - 'ana kaynağa dokunulmamış olurdu' (Kars 167), 'Vakfedilen paranın aslına dokunulmaksızın işletilmesi' (Kars 179), 'Ana paradan harcama yapılmaması esası benimsenmiştir', with officials who spend principal made to restore it (Küçük 151); the kadı instructs the trustee to lend the remainder 'asl-ı mâl olmak üzere' (Kıvrım 48); preserving principal is the trustee's first duty in EMM deeds generally (Gürsoy 110). No donor or resident withdraws. Erosion happened - 55 kuruş 'vakıf paradan noksan' in the 1844 accounts (Küçük 154) - but erosion is not withdrawal at will.

No source says whether a resident's claim on the fund could be alienated. Benefit follows residence ('mahalle sükkanına', Kars 175) and donors could tie an exemption to their own houses (Kıvrım 37); a plot 'avarıza bağlı' carried a 200 akçe annual payment to the quarter's avarız through a sale (Kars 178) - an obligation running with land, the reverse of a transferable interest. Not 0.
Follows CI3: nothing on transferable, let alone depersonalised, interests.

CF1 is 0, locator members. The fund's obligations to third parties are never described, so residents' liability for them is not addressed. Residents shared the unfunded remainder of the levy (Kars 167; Kıvrım 37): their tax, not the fund's debt. EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not 'none' (priors, exposure item 3).

The decision-maker is the mütevelli, who lends (Küçük 150). Where his pay is stated it is a fixed salary - 150 kuruş a year against 942 kuruş nema (Küçük 154) - and his exposure is fault-based: officials who spend principal must restore it (Küçük 151); a trustee lending without pledge or surety is removed (Gürsoy 110, an EMM deed of 1671 not identified as an avarız fund). Nothing shows him bearing borrowers' defaults. Counter-instance: the Burdur deed gives the mütevelli 75 of the 375 akçe stipulated profit (Kars 176), a fixed share of an expected return. Low; alternative .NR, since no source asks whether the trustee bore losses. Trustees also borrowed from their own funds (Kıvrım 43; Küçük 173) - insider credit, not coupling.

No return proportional to contribution: income goes to the quarter's levy, its poor, funerals, the imam and public works (Kars 167, 175-176; Küçük 154). Donors take nothing back except, in two Ayntab deeds, the exemption of their own house (Kıvrım 37) - a fixed condition, not a share.

Structurally half-present within one fund. The main line pays the quarter's avarız, a levy assessed on the tax unit as the taxable households' 'ortak bir sorumluluğu' (Kars 167); income meets it for everyone and residents split the remainder (Kars 167; Kıvrım 37) - relief of a common burden, not mutualisation of a member's misfortune. The other lines are contingent on member-specific hazard: the poor's share of the levy ('mahalle fukarası avarızı', Kars 175-176; 272 kuruş for poor residents' tax debts and 200 for poor funerals, Küçük 154; 250 kuruş for the poor's 1866 avarız, Küçük 161) and an interest-free loan from the sum endowed 'mahalle ahalisinin afet durumunda kullanabilmesi için' to a resident whose house burned (Kars 184). Contributors are partly residents ('mahalle halkının katkılarıyla', Kıvrım 37; the residents' own aid chest, Küçük 152) and partly notables, which blurs mutualisation into allocation. Gürsoy 124's likening of the sandıks to pension and unemployment insurance is the author's analogy and founds nothing here. Alternatives: 1 (the begijnhof reading) and 0 (the fund as charity allocated to residents). EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not P, and a 2026-08-19 logbook passage read the pooling as sitting in the residual tax (priors, exposure items 3 and 5); this cell disagrees with the first and reads the same evidence differently from the second.

LR4 is not 0, so the cell exists. The baskets are households' capacity to meet their share of the levy, and the levy rose for all at once in wartime (Kars 169, foundations peaking in 1661-64 and 1688-89 with the Habsburg, Persian and Polish wars; Küçük 148 on the levy becoming annual and monetised). A house fire is idiosyncratic, but the fund's dominant draw falls on everyone together. Low.
LR2 is veiled: no directional exposure of the decision-maker to characterise.

Residents claim as the deeds' designated beneficiaries - the quarter's residents or its poor ('mahalle sükkanına', 'mahalle fukarası avarızı', Kars 175-176; 'Ammu Mahallesi fukarasının menzil ve avârızlarına', Kıvrım 37) - not by admission and not by contract. Borrowers, many from outside the quarter (Küçük 157-160; Kıvrım 39), are counterparties, not entitlement holders. Alternative membership: residence, and residents' choice of trustee, resemble membership, but no admission or roll is described.

Residents choose the trustee and register him before the kadı: Kanalıcı and Kayser residents name their mütevelli in court (Kıvrım 38, GŞS 15/489, 32-10/3); a bölük trustee is 'ahali-i mahalle-i mezbûre talebiyle mütevelli nasb ve tayin olunan', and the Kızılca Mescid residents inspect the ledger, are 'râzı ve şâkir' with the trustee and choose him again (Kıvrım 47-48, transcriptions); the 1867 Kırkçeşme trustee receives the bonds 'muhtaran ve ihtiyaran marifetleriyle' (Küçük 160 n.56). Kars 173 states the rule in Kıvrım's own sentence and is not a second witness. Uses are fixed by founders' conditions (Kars 175) and lending is the trustee's under the kadı (Küçük 150-151): collective at the level of appointment and oversight.
MG1 is beneficiary: there is no membership whose entry could be restricted.

Constituted as vakıf under fiqh and confirmed by the kadı: 'Vakıf tasdik olunur' (Kars 176); a nukud vakfı founded 'İmam Züfer kavli ile' (Kars 175); vakfiyes approved in the Evkaf Muhasebeciliği court (Gürsoy 96-97). Alternative customary: Küçük 149-151 reports Ebussuud defending cash waqfs on örf, 'kıstasın örf olduğuna vurgu yapmıştır', so the religious-law authorisation itself rested on custom. HAZARD: MG4=religious has been criticised in this census when coded for consistency with waqf_khayri; this value rests on the kadı's confirmation of each deed, not on that analogy.

Both halves declared in the same deeds and accounts. Mutual: a fund for the quarter's own common levy and expenditure - 'mahalle ve köy sakinlerinin ortak harcamalarına kaynaklık edecek bir fon' (Küçük 148), 'mahalle sakinlerinin kolektif harcamaları için' (Küçük 153). Pious-charitable: the same funds pay the mescid imam, Ramazan recitation, 'suleha-yı fukara' and a sıbyan mektebi (Kars 175-177; Küçük 154); donors are 'hayır sahipleri' (Kıvrım 37) and Kars calls the institution 'hayrî bir kuruluş' (185). Alternative mutual-provision, if the levy line is taken as primary.
No source discusses any franchise or exclusive right held by a fund. A bakery and serhane served as income for one quarter's avarız (Kars 174); whether either carried a franchise is not stated.

No status or access arbitrage is described. The nearest facts - donors' own houses exempted from avarız by condition (Kıvrım 37), non-Muslims founding, managing and borrowing (Kars 177-178) - do not make the fund a status wrapper.

Registered and audited: trustees registered in court on residents' request (Kıvrım 38; Kars 173); loans and sale-leasebacks registered in the şer'î courts (Kars 180); in 1692 nine Ayntab funds' accounts entered in the sicil (Kıvrım 39); vakfiyes confirmed in a court established to control waqf accounts (Gürsoy 96-97); Kırkçeşme's accounts examined before the kadı and the fund entered in the 1844 Evkaf defter (Küçük 151, 154-155).

No party to the arrangement supplies labour against another's capital: donors endow, residents benefit, and management is by an elected trustee paid a salary (Küçük 154) or, in one deed, a fixed share of the stipulated profit (Kars 176). Borrowers are debtors, not partners. Low: the trustee's labour against donors' capital could be read as P, and .NA (the waqf_khayri disposition) is the other alternative.
CF1 is 0: there is no labour-supplying party whose bearing of capital loss could be asked about.

Many donors and many beneficiaries per fund: several endowments collected into one quarter's sandık (Gürsoy 105); funds 'mahalle halkının katkılarıyla kurulmuş ve çeşitli vesilelerle yapılan bağışlarla zenginleştirilmiştir' (Kıvrım 37; Kars 169 repeats the sentence); later sadaka added to the Kırkçeşme fund (Küçük 157).

Klieber never puts the question of juridical personhood. 'korporative Akteure' (36) is organisation-theory vocabulary, not a legal finding; approval by the church authority gave official status, title, indulgences and supervision (50); an 1866 ministerial note subjected confraternities to the association law while exempting them from the register (68). None of this says whether a fraternity was a legal person distinct from its members.

Fraternities held and disposed of property as fraternities: assets surveyed per association (348,348 fl across 143 in 1760, 42), fraternities as 'Inhaber eigener Kirchen' (55), capital lent on Schuldbriefe (56), purchases 'aus Eigenmitteln' (59), and the Josefsbruderschaft's consilium resolving in 1774 to cede 'Zwölftausend Sechs Gulden Capital schanckungsweise [...] zu cediren' to the Sebastian house (58). For 'betreute' fraternities finances lay with abbots or superiors (52) - administration, not ownership. Enlightenment governments diverted fraternity capital (59), which presupposes it was theirs. Articulated on the 1774 resolution's own words. Alternative P, on the betreute subtype.
Litigation by or against a fraternity is not reported. Debt collection ran through the Pfleggerichte's 'Amtshilfe' (57), which is not standing.
Creditors of a fraternity, and their rank against members' creditors, are never mentioned; fraternities appear only as lenders (56-57).

Members could stop paying and so drop out, forfeiting the promised services (48); one could 'nur gewinnen, jedoch nichts verlieren' by joining (49). Nothing on withdrawing contributions, and nothing at all on members' creditors. Creditor limb silent: .NR.
CF1 is 0, locator members. Whether a creditor of a fraternity could reach a member's estate is not addressed.

No founder whose patrimony constitutes the corpus. Fraternities arise by initiative, erection and ecclesiastical approval (Klieber 2001, 38, 50), and their means come from entry gifts, contributions, collections, legacies and interest (48, 59); donors and Stifterinnen add to an existing body (63) and none constitutes it. On AP4's definition that is .NA, not 0. EXPOSURE: the bundle's AP4 definition implies one form under re-coding carries AP4=1 live (priors, exposure item 1).

Built to outlive its members: the service is to members after death (42-43); several Salzburg associations have more than 300 years' documented existence (37); the Liebesbünde depended on a continuing age pyramid of members (45).
No term: Remling's criterion 'auf Dauer angelegte' is Klieber's starting point (35), and associations run from the 17th into the 20th century (37-38).

Fraternities were ended from outside - Josephinist dissolution in the Austrian hereditary lands (53, not Salzburg), loss of independence in Salzburg c.1780-1820 (38), a Liebesbund dissolved in 1926 against members' wishes by an authority not named (46), NS dissolution orders 1938-41 (68) - but Klieber does not show a party to the arrangement holding a power to dissolve it at will. Individual exit (48) is not dissolution.

Half-present. Independent fraternities ran their own affairs and finances (52, 66) and by internal decision took on new ends: the Dreifaltigkeitsbruderschaft's alms to Hausarme from 1766 and the Josefsbruderschaft consilium's 1774 gift of capital to the Sebastian house, 'hülfreiche Hand zubiethen' (58); a Liebesbund reserved up to ten per cent for alms 'freiwillig' (58). But statutes needed approval by the church authority (50), and foundations for special liturgies the consistory's consent (55). Low. EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not 1 (priors, exposure item 3).

One purse per fraternity: assets per association (42), capital lent out (56), interest income per fraternity (59); Liebesbünde financed their masses from fixed contributions or ad hoc 'im Umlaufsystem' (45). A contribution rate reserved for Hausarme in one Liebesbund (57-58) is an earmark within the purse.
Nothing on whether members could reclaim contributions. Ceasing to pay meant de facto exit and the loss of the promised services (48); refund is never mentioned.

Membership is by personal enrolment in a book (44, 49); transfer of membership is never discussed. Admission of a deceased person on contributions paid by the living (47) is enrolment by proxy, not transfer.
Follows CI3: nothing on depersonalised interests.
CF1 is 0, locator members. Members' liability for a fraternity's obligations to third parties is not addressed. EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not 'none' (priors, exposure item 3).

The decision-makers are the prefect, consilium and administrator of independent fraternities, or the religious superior of 'betreute' ones (52). Whether they bore any of the fraternity's outcomes is not addressed; the only exposure mentioned runs the other way - administrators who were merchants profited as suppliers (56). Officers sat for life and accounts were signed by a small committee (67).

Returns are fixed services, not shares of a surplus: every sister received 'die gleichen totendienstlichen Leistungen wie ein Mitbruder' (66); Liebesbünde guaranteed a set number of masses against fixed contributions (45, 48).

Mutualisation of a member-specific hazard, and the author's central finding. Each member's death is met from a common fund built by the living: fraternities as 'Totenbünde' offering a 'versicherungsartig garantierter Dienst der Lebenden an den Toten' that came to each member 'in einer Art Umlagesystem bzw. Generationenvertrag' (42-43); Liebesbünde guaranteeing a set number of masses at death, financed by fixed contributions or ad hoc 'im Umlaufsystem', whose 'versicherungsartige Struktur' failed when entries fell and the age pyramid tipped (45); the purpose restated as 'Eigenvorsorge fürs Jenseits' through a 'versicherungsartigem Zusammenschluß' (62-63). The hazard is the timing of death and its spiritual consequence, met with masses, burial, bier and shroud (43-44). Material relief of living members was slight - 'nur gering ausgeprägt' (57), about eight per cent of contributions as alms in one Liebesbund (58 n.37) - and does not carry the value. Analyst-imposed: 'versicherungsartig' and 'Umlagesystem' are Klieber's words. Alternative P, if spiritual provision is held to fall outside the characteristic; the definition does not restrict the currency. EXPOSURE: priors item 4 recorded a prior session's reading of Klieber as relief-marginal; this cell agrees on relief and rests on the Totendienst.

LR4 is not 0. The baskets are members' deaths, which fall at different times; the Liebesbünde's solvency depended on a steady inflow of new members against an ageing membership (45) - a demographic exposure, not a common shock. No epidemic is discussed. Low.
LR2 is .NR, so applicability cannot be settled; .NA would assert LR2=veiled (the begijnhof disposition).
Entitlement rests on enrolment: entry in the Bruderschaftsbuch or the issue of a Zettel sufficed for the post-mortem services (49), which every enrolled member received equally (66).

Independent fraternities elected their heads - prefect, assistants, consilium - and steered their affairs and finances 'weitgehend autonom' for nearly two centuries (52, 66); women were excluded from these elections (65), officers often sat for life and accounts were signed by a small committee (67). But 'betreute' fraternities were run by abbots, superiors or rectors (52), and after c.1785 the restrictions withdrew administration and left the fraternities to the parish clergy (53). The row spans collective and single-principal across both subtypes and its period; the value records the independent type of 1600-c.1785, which Klieber says dominated the countryside (53). Phase split proposed in the notes file; low for that reason.

Free access is one of Klieber's defining criteria and approving authorities demanded it: 'vor alle Christglaubige beyderley Geschlechts [...] ohne Ausnahme des Mindesten oder Schlechtesten derselben' (48, quoting enrolment slips); poverty clauses kept fees from excluding (48). The Liebesbünde's fixed contributions 'schränkten das Prinzip des freien Zugangs ein', applied leniently (48) - a difference between subtypes, not a structural half. Occupational fraternities are the stated exception (47). EXPOSURE: logbook 4 implies the live value is not P (priors, exposure item 3).

Official status required approval by the competent church authority, with effect on title, indulgences, statutes and supervision (50); Trent made the bishops competent (47-48 and n.23); indulgences were granted by Rome (46).

Primary purpose: service to the members' own dead. Every one of more than three dozen associations was explicitly devoted to it and many to nothing else (43); the definition names 'geistig-geistlicher Fonds' for the members' good death, burial and purgatory (50); the purpose was 'optimale Eigenvorsorge fürs Jenseits' (62), 'Zukunftsvorsorge [...] mittels versicherungsartigem Zusammenschluß' (63). Charity was 'nur gering ausgeprägt' and Klieber rejects the 'religiös-karitativ' formula (57). Against: contemporaries understood care for the dead as an act of Nächstenliebe (59), and the 1917 Code gave Gottesdienstmehrung as the Proprium (35) - the pious-charitable reading, held as the alternative; mixed is the other. Analyst-imposed: the 'mutual' reading is the author's.

Indulgence and altar privileges (46) and the Dreifaltigkeitsbruderschaft's privilege to beg the release of one condemned person each Good Friday (61) are privileges; whether any was held as property, or was exclusive in a franchise sense, is not addressed.

Membership 'sich als Nachweis der konfessionellen Zuverlässigkeit eignete' (47) and rural boards were their communities' only elected spokesmen (67), but Klieber does not show membership conferring a legal status or access its principals could not otherwise have. One clause, not a finding.

Legible without a register. Statutes and accounts were subject to approval and annual accounting to the ordinary (48 n.23, 66), money dealings were increasingly controlled by the consistory (56-57), and official surveys of 1760 and 1771 counted fraternities and their assets (42) - and in the prince-archbishopric ecclesiastical and political authority coincided. But no authority, church or state, ever had a complete overview (68), and an 1866 ministerial note exempted fraternities from keeping a Kataster (68). Half-present.
Members are alike: all receive the same services (66); a small group of officers ran the liturgy (49), and chaplains, sacristans and collectors were employees (57). No capital-labour asymmetry.
CF1 is 0: there is no labour-supplying party whose bearing of capital loss could be asked about.
Many members: about 50,000 enrolments a decade across the city's fraternities (40), 148,835 in one scapular confraternity 1632-1958 (46), 15,570 in the Annabruderschaft 1619-1903 (64).
